title: A file API that does more than upload

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Some projects are named for their first job and then quietly grow. SpringBootFilesUploader started as a way to upload files, and ended up as a small control console for a server.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Let's start at the beginning. What does the upload part do?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's a Kotlin API built on Spring Boot. You send it a file, it puts the bytes in an S3-compatible bucket, which can be MinIO, and it stores the file's description in MongoDB. Later you ask for the file by its id and it hands it back.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why split it in two places?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Each store does what it's good at. The bucket holds the heavy content under a unique folder name, and the database keeps the light information: name, extension, content type and size. That makes lookups fast and keeps downloads simple.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Everything sits behind JWT authentication with three roles. Moderators and admins can upload, any signed-in user can download, and only an admin can create another admin account. The upload also checks the file extension against a list that covers spreadsheets, Word documents, PDFs, common images, video, audio and archives.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: You said it grew beyond uploads. How?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The same application also drives Docker. Through the Docker Engine, it can list containers, create them, start, stop, restart and rename them. Moderators and admins can handle most of that, while creating and renaming is reserved for admins.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So a web request can start a container?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. It also pings a Caddy server through its admin interface, and it can run commands on remote machines over SSH, which is restricted to admins. All of it is described in an OpenAPI page generated automatically, so you can explore the endpoints.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It sounds like a Swiss army knife for a home server.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's a fair picture. The code is organized in clean layers, with controllers, services and repositories, and the page lists the six controllers and what each one is allowed to do.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Where do I find the details?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In the written page. It has a diagram of the whole upload and download flow, the project structure and the external services it expects, with the default addresses.
